researcher: Codex parallel africa-regional-kingdoms research, integrated by Codex

sources.title: Giacomo Macola: A political history of the Kingdom of Kazembe, Zambia
sources.note: Doctoral research abstract: eighteenth and nineteenth century regional influence, lower Luapula heartland, institutions and colonial transition. Indexed abstract accessible; direct page failed.

sources.title: David Livingstone: Last Journals in Central Africa
sources.note: Dated primary observations at Kazembe in November 1867 to January 1868. Perspective is a visiting missionary’s, not a survey of every household.

sources.title: Mwansabombwe Town Council: About Mwansabombwe
sources.note: Local institutional history and cultural continuity. Origin narrative is labelled as tradition; disputed 1760 location of capital is not used.

sources.title: David M. Gordon: History on the Luapula Retold
sources.note: 2006 original research abstract on landscape, shrines, historical memory and Lunda and Shila identities.

sources.title: David Gordon: Owners of the Land and Lunda Lords
sources.note: 2001 research article summarized by African Studies Centre Leiden. Checked Kazembe defeat in 1899 and negotiated continuity only; abstract has an erroneous 1895 date for Msiri, which is excluded.

sources.title: University of Zambia: Cultural tourism and the Umutomboko ceremony, 1961 to 2017
sources.note: Indexed thesis passages checked on government support in 1971 and expansion of public ceremony; direct PDF timed out.

sources.title: Robert Cancel: Storytelling in Northern Zambia
sources.note: 2013 original field research, chapter V, Lunda storytelling. Indexed passage for Idon Pandwe’s Kalulu garden tale checked; publisher direct page has bot challenge.

sources.title: Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina, Instituto Kadila: África Geral catalogue
sources.note: Catalogue entry 81 verifies Portuguese title O Muata Cazembe and author António Cândido Pedroso Gamito, 1937 edition of expedition account. It is a visitor’s language, not a local manuscript.

sources.title: Royal Museum for Central Africa: The Yeke and the Congo Free State
sources.note: Museum historical analysis of Msiri, trade, 1891 confrontation and successor’s colonial collaboration. Conflicting death accounts acknowledged; graphic details excluded.

sources.title: Royal Museum for Central Africa: Bunkeya Plurielle
sources.note: Research project description: nineteenth-century capital, long copper history and collaboration with communities and University of Lubumbashi. Project objectives are not reported as completed discoveries.

sources.title: Nicolas Nikis: Central African Copper
sources.note: Oxford Research Encyclopedia article in author repository. Indexed detailed smelting passage checked; direct PDF redirects to repository error. Later reenactments by Yeke smelters are dated as such.

sources.title: Across the Copperbelt: Kingdoms and Associations, copper’s nineteenth-century political economy
sources.note: Chapter 6, indexed page 172 and adjoining text: copper, ivory monopoly, trade networks and migration myth. Direct PDF returns 403.

sources.title: Royal Museum for Central Africa: Haut-Katanga, volume 1
sources.note: Section 3, L’empire Yeke du Katanga-Garenganze: migration, heterogeneous caravans, marriage and incorporation.

sources.title: Mwami Msiri royal heritage site: Chants Yeke
sources.note: Modern published Yeke song collection with French translations. Indexed complete page checked; direct access timed out. Tiny title sample only, no claim of nineteenth-century written date.

sources.title: Rachel Taylor, University of Oxford: Beyond the Male Gaze, images of Katangese women
sources.note: Research discussion begins with Maria de Fonseca image from 1893 travel publication; used for visual source perspective, not as evidence for twentieth-century mining households under Msiri.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Sahel, inside the exhibition
sources.note: Bamana Segu section. Avoid disputed precise accession date for Ngolo Diarra.

sources.title: Mungo Park: Travels in the Interior Districts of Africa
sources.note: Chapter XV, July 1796. Eyewitness account mediated by a European visitor; estimates and sweeping character judgments excluded.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Headdress, Male, Ci Wara, 1978.412.436
sources.note: Nineteenth to early twentieth century object and contextual account of agricultural performance.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Genesis, Ideas of Origin in African Sculpture
sources.note: Bamana social and agricultural context, page 14; not a claim that every custom is documented in eighteenth-century Segu.

sources.title: University of Michigan Museum of Art: Mother and child figure
sources.note: Late nineteenth to early twentieth century Bamana figure, 2016/1.250. Cultural continuity, not an object securely from the independent kingdom.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Power object, boli, 1979.206.81
sources.note: Early twentieth century central Mali object; explicitly later evidence.

sources.title: Peace Corps Mali: An Introduction to Bambara
sources.note: Modern Latin orthography. Greeting checked on PDF page 5, family vocabulary on page 3.

sources.title: Rıza Kurtuluş: Bagirmi, TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi
sources.note: Political chronology and regional location; published 1991. Early chronology is approximate and competing oral traditions exist.

sources.title: Annie M.-D. Lebeuf: Boum Massénia, capitale de l’ancien royaume du Baguirmi
sources.note: Journal des Africanistes 37(2), 1967, opening page 215 checked: old Massenya, surviving walls and brickwork, abandonment in 1898.

sources.title: Heinrich Barth: Travels and Discoveries, volume 3
sources.note: 1857 publication of 1852 observations. Faki Sambo, court offices, crafts and languages; exclude the author’s racial judgments.

sources.title: Viviana Pâques: Origine et caractères du pouvoir royal au Baguirmi
sources.note: 1967 study, page 183: research missions of 1966 and 1967, competing oral and written chronologies.

sources.title: Church of the Lutheran Brethren: Kup an Duniya, The Beginning of Creation
sources.note: Modern Bagirmi-language Christian publication. Title and translation are publisher-attested; distinguish from sultanate-era Islamic manuscripts.

sources.title: Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe: Old Bulawayo
sources.note: Institutional history and reconstruction. Dates of museum reconstructions are not dates of original structures.

sources.title: National Museums and Monuments of Zimbabwe: Western Region, Bulawayo
sources.note: Old Bulawayo site, Indaba tree, settlement layout and Jesuit mission.

sources.title: Robert Tendai Nyamushosho: Ceramic ethnoarchaeology in Zimbabwe
sources.note: 2014 research discussion, page 20, including Khumalo 2013 Old Bulawayo study. Modern comparative uses distinguished from excavated objects.

sources.title: Liz Stanley, University of Edinburgh: Letters by Njube
sources.note: Transcribed September and October 1898 letters in Rhodes Papers. The original fore spelling is preserved. Do not use the page’s problematic dating of war negotiations.

sources.title: Aberdeen Archives, Gallery and Museums: Matabele straining spoon
sources.note: Wooden spoon, 22.7 by 5.3 cm, Robert Williams bequest 1946. No precise manufacture date supplied.

sources.title: Paul H. Gundani: The just war tradition in Zimbabwean historiography
sources.note: 2019 historical analysis, section on the 1893 British South Africa Company war of conquest.

sources.title: TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi: Futa Calon
sources.note: Formation, federal institutions, Alfaya and Soriya rivalry and 1896 conquest. Founding dates differ in scholarship; use early eighteenth century.

sources.title: Boubacar Barry: Futa Jallon expansion into the Southern Rivers region
sources.note: Chapter abstract: commercial expansion, peanut exports and coastal routes in the nineteenth century.

sources.title: Winston McGowan: Fula resistance to French expansion into Futa Jallon, 1889 to 1896
sources.note: Research abstract: diplomatic strategies, European rivalries and internal divisions.

sources.title: Les rapports Nord-Sud, la traite négrière et le Fuuta Jaloo à la fin du XVIIIe siècle
sources.note: Historical research on slave labour and the slave trade in the eighteenth-century state.

sources.title: Boston University NEH Ajami: Knowledge to Follow God
sources.note: Undated Arabic and Fuuta Jalon Fula manuscript owned by El Hadj Mouhamadou Sall, provenance Conakry, digitized in 2016. Do not assign it to the independent imamate.

sources.title: Ngom and colleagues: Knowledge to Follow God, English translation
sources.note: 2022 scholarly translation, pages 1 to 3 for washing and dry ablution. Same underlying manuscript as catalogue and transcription; aggregate budget checked.

sources.title: Ngom and colleagues: Gandal Fii Rewugol Alla, transcription
sources.note: Page 1: ndiyaŋ laaɓuɗaŋ, corresponding to clean water. Roman transcription, not a facsimile of Ajami handwriting.

sources.title: Luc Descroix and colleagues: Hydrological role of intensive agriculture in Fouta Djalon
sources.note: 2022 field-based research abstract. Current crop combinations are not backdated to the eighteenth century.

sources.title: Boston University Anthropology: Digital preservation of Fuuta Jalon manuscripts
sources.note: February 2026 project completion: 49 collections, 52,415 pages, some eighteenth century.

sources.title: National Humanities Center: The African Homeland of Abdul Rahman Ibrahima
sources.note: 2009 teaching edition of Cyrus Griffin’s 1828 newspaper account. Use editorial biography and clearly attributed recollection; exclude racial assertions and implausible unsupported political claims.

sources.title: Andrew F. Clark: Futa-Tooro, Encyclopedia of African History
sources.note: Academic encyclopedia entry reproduced by community scholarly library webPulaaku. Page heading correctly identifies Andrew F. Clark despite misleading page metadata.

sources.title: Wendell Marsh: Reading with the colonial in the life of Shaykh Musa Kamara
sources.note: 2020 original research. Biographical sketch: 1776 formation, nineteenth-century autonomy, education and Arabic scholarship.

sources.title: Library of Congress: New Omar Ibn Said Story Map
sources.note: Institutional biography: Futa Toro origin, capture, American enslavement and 1831 autobiography.

sources.title: Carl W. Ernst and Mbaye Lo: Omar ibn Said, autobiography transcription
sources.note: Scholarly Arabic transcription linked to LOC original 2018371864. Original page 14, line 59: اسمي عمر بن سيد.

sources.title: Library of Congress: Isaac Bird translation of Omar ibn Said’s life
sources.note: Historical English translation with Adam Rothman transcription. Image 5 describes birthplace and twenty-five years of learning; geographical gloss is not repeated.

sources.title: Sylvia Albro, Library of Congress: Conserving a one-of-a-kind manuscript
sources.note: Conservator’s account of damaged binding, repairs and preservation.

sources.title: James Courtright: Droughts, dams and food security in Futa Toro
sources.note: 2022 first-person field reporting and named interviews. Childhood memories explicitly dated to the twentieth century, not retrojected into the imamate.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Shared narrative for two phases of Bagirmi Sultanate. First map coverage 1530 to 1700; second 1783 to 1815. Second geometry lies south of old Massenya at 11 degrees 33 minutes north, 16 degrees 40 minutes east. It is not evidence for a separate southern sultanate. Preserve imported geography limitation.
Imported 1715 to 1815 interval is partial coverage; historical Bamana kingdom approximately 1712 to 1861. Later imported polygons are broad, extending far beyond core Niger towns.
Imported 1815 to 1878 polygon lies well south and east of the lower Luapula heartland and 1867 court. Do not claim geometry repaired or relocate the historical narrative to the bad polygon.
Imported 1878 to 1914 interval is later than formation and extends beyond 1896 conquest. Distinct from Futa Toro.
Imported 1878 to 1914 polygon extends south of the middle Senegal River heartland. Nineteenth-century autonomy eroded gradually; avoid treating one disputed terminal year as a sudden disappearance.
Zimbabwe geometry identifies northern Ndebele kingdom, not South African Ndebele communities. Historical 1893 conquest precedes imported 1914 cutoff.
Katanga geometry supports Yeke / Garenganze identity. Msiri’s 1891 death and loss of independence precede imported 1914 cutoff.
